newsitem.title: UK: London gold picks up at fixing, but tone still weak.
newsitem.headline: London gold picks up at fixing, but tone still weak.

text.p: Light short covering after gold prices held around 3-1/4 year lows on Wednesday morning helped the bullion market pare overnight losses, dealers said.
"It's still very bearish. We are still looking for further losses," a dealer said.
Bullion fixed at $356.60 per ounce Wednesday afternoon after $355.80 in the morning and $359.00 on Tuesday afternoon.
The morning fix was just above the lowest since October 6, 1993 when it was $353.50. Gold has traced a 3.25-percent price slide since the start of the year when market weakness began to accelerate.

Fresh selling snuffed out Tuesday's feeble rally overnight. "It was the same old story. The rally on Tuesday was just taken as an excuse to sell and take a profit," one dealer said. Dealers said a report from an authoritative research group, Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS), that gold sales from the official sector had accelerated in the second half of 1996 was a major factor weakening the price.
GFMS said 123 tonnes were sold by offical institutions -- usually assumed to be central banks -- in that period to give an estimated total of 208 tonnes of gold sold during the year.
But some market sources were doubtful.
"How do they know that? There has been no announcement, just lots of rumours," a senior dealer said.

Dealers said the fear central bank and International Monetary Fund sales had undermined confidence in bullion. "The professionals are selling short this morning and the funds were involved earlier this week," a dealer said.
"There are a few little physical orders coming through under the market but they will not be enough to stem another flood of selling," the dealer added.
Bullion market analyst Andy Smith at Union Bank of Switzerland said a major reason for the weak gold price was selling by put option writers as the price slipped.
"Once the option strangle was broken the selling produced an accelerator effect on the price fall," Smith said.

Palladium was the only precious metal to show any steadiness. It was down only 25 cents at $120.00/$121.00 while platinum was indicated at $359.50/$360.50, down near $2.80 and silver shed five cents to $4.66/44.68.
Palladium was being supported by consumer and speculative buying against Russia delaying its January shipments to Japan, the world's largest consumer of the metal, dealers said.
